path.id: The non-compete clause defines "competing tools" broadly as any software, platform, or service that provides functionality substantially similar to any feature offered by the vendor. This definition lacks specificity and could encompass general-purpose tools such as spreadsheet applications, project management software, or communication platforms that share minor functional overlap with the vendor's product.

Section 7.3 requires the client to submit a written declaration of all software tools in use at the time of contract signing. Any tools not declared are automatically subject to the non-compete restriction upon termination, creating a compliance burden and potential inadvertent breach.

Third, there is no geographic limitation, effectively making this a global restriction. I would recommend narrowing the scope to direct competitors only, reducing the restriction period to 6â12 months, and adding a carve-out for tools already in use at the time of signing. The enforceability of such broad non-compete clauses varies significantly by jurisdiction.

The survival clause in Section 9.2 states that non-compete obligations persist even if the vendor materially breaches the agreement. This is atypical and potentially unenforceable in several jurisdictions, as courts generally require mutual consideration for post-termination restrictions to remain valid.

Yes, the non-compete clause can be revised to create a more balanced and enforceable structure. Typically, this involves narrowing the definition of competing tools to named direct competitors, limiting the restriction period to 6â12 months, adding geographic boundaries, and including a carve-out for pre-existing tools. It is also important to ensure that the restriction is mutual rather than one-sided, so both parties share responsibility fairly. I can draft a revised version that incorporates these changes while maintaining legal clarity and enforceability.

Additionally, the liquidated damages provision in Section 7.5 should be reviewed. Courts in many jurisdictions require that liquidated damages bear a reasonable relationship to anticipated actual damages. A penalty of 150% of the remaining contract value may be deemed punitive and therefore unenforceable. A more defensible approach would be to cap damages at actual provable losses or a reasonable estimate thereof.

The non-compete clause in Section 7 contains several provisions that warrant attention. First, it imposes a 24-month restriction on using competing SaaS platforms after contract termination, which is unusually broad for a vendor agreement. Second, the definition of "competing tools" is vague and could be interpreted to include any software with overlapping functionality. Third, there is no geographic limitation, effectively making this a global restriction. I would recommend narrowing the scope to direct competitors only, reducing the restriction period to 6â12 months, and adding a carve-out for tools already in use at the time of signing.
